title: Walk modestly, lower your voice
hook: don't turn your cheek in scorn, walk modestly, lower your voice (31:18–19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother's burden, and your line was remember what was carried. Did you send the line of thanks, or say the prayer? Day five hundred thirty-five.

Some people announce their own importance before they say a word. The way they walk into a room, taking up the middle of the corridor. The way they half-turn their face away when someone they consider beneath them starts talking. The volume on the phone call in the train carriage. Luqman's advice to his son ends not with doctrine but with exactly this: how to hold your face, how to walk, and how loud to be.

Luqman has told his son to pray, to enjoin what's right, to forbid what's wrong, and to be patient with what befalls him. Then he gets physical. Pickthall: "Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land." The Arabic for turning the cheek is tusa''ir khaddak. Classical lexicons say the root sa'ar was a condition in camels that made them twist their necks to one side. So the picture is a person whose head is permanently turned away from others, as if they're not worth facing. And walking with pertness is marahan, strutting, walking in exultation. God doesn't love, the verse says, every arrogant boaster. Then the positive version. Pickthall: "Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice." The first word is iqsid, from the same root as qasd, the middle, moderation. Not crawling and not strutting. A steady pace, aimed somewhere. And lower your voice, ughdud, the same verb used in the Qur'an for lowering the gaze. Then comes a line that sticks: the harshest of all voices, the verse says, is the braying of the donkey. Loudness for its own sake isn't strength; it's just noise. This isn't a rule against ever raising your voice. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called out to warn, and the call to prayer is meant to carry. It's about posture toward people: a face that turns toward them, a walk that doesn't take over the street, and a voice sized to the room.
screen: `TURN NOT THY CHEEK IN SCORN.` · `NO STRUTTING IN THE LAND.` · `IQSID: THE STEADY MIDDLE PACE.` · `LOWER YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak softly today. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your face right now: is it turned toward anything, or away? Let it soften. Then think of the place where you're usually loudest: the kitchen, a meeting, the car, a group chat in capital letters. Picture the same moment with your voice brought down by half and your face turned toward the other person. Notice whether anything gets lost. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle voice. The bell holds the time.
Walk modestly. Luqman's advice on how to carry yourself: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut, keep a steady pace, and lower your voice. Today's word.
Your line: lower your voice. Today, in the place you're usually loudest, try saying the same thing at half the volume. Day five hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often teach Luqman's last pieces of advice, 31:17–19, as a short guide to manners: prayer, patience, humility, a moderate walk and a lowered voice.

what a scholar hears: tusa''ir from sa'ar, the camel's twisted neck; iqsid from qasd; and ughdud, the verb also used for lowering the gaze (24:30–31).

notes: Pickthall 31:18–19 quoted from memory; confirm wording.
Sa'ar as a camel's neck condition is in the classical lexicons and commentaries (e.g. al-Tabari); confirm.
Ughdud in 31:19 shares the verb gh-d-d with yaghuddu in 24:30–31 (lowering the gaze): confirm.
The Prophet 'called out to warn' is unsourced in the script (the Safa call, Bukhari 4770, is the likely reference); confirm or cite.
